nodes.concept: Even/odd (parity) basics
nodes.description: Integers are either even or odd. The sum of two integers has predictable parity: even+even=even, odd+odd=even, and even+odd=odd. These rules are often used to deduce constraints without knowing exact values.

nodes.concept: Parity of prime numbers
nodes.description: All prime numbers except 2 are odd. The number 2 is the unique even prime. So if a prime is even, it must be 2.

nodes.concept: Equal-sum constraint on two-sided cards
nodes.description: If each card has a number on each side and all cards have the same sum of (front + back), then there exists a single constant S such that each card’s front number plus its hidden back number equals S. This turns the situation into a system of equations with a common sum. Knowing any pair (front, back) determines S.

nodes.concept: Problem instantiation: visible numbers and hidden primes
nodes.description: In this specific problem, the visible numbers are 44, 59, and 38, and each card has a hidden number on the other side. The hidden numbers are given to be prime numbers. All three cards share the same (visible + hidden) sum.

nodes.concept: Identify parity of the visible numbers
nodes.description: Among the visible numbers, 44 and 38 are even while 59 is odd. So there are two even visible numbers and one odd visible number. This parity pattern will constrain the parity of the hidden numbers and of the common sum.

nodes.concept: Parity constraint on the common sum S
nodes.description: Because each card’s sum equals the same S, all three (visible + hidden) sums must have the same parity. Adding an even visible number to a prime hidden number yields an odd sum if the hidden prime is odd, and an even sum only if the hidden prime is 2. Adding an odd visible number to an odd prime yields an even sum, but adding an odd visible number to 2 yields an odd sum.

nodes.concept: Deduce which hidden prime must be 2
nodes.description: If the hidden primes opposite 44 and 38 were odd (as most primes are), then their sums would be odd (even+odd=odd). To match that parity, the sum on the 59-card must also be odd, which can only happen if the hidden prime there is 2 (odd+2=odd). Therefore, 2 must be paired with 59.

nodes.concept: Compute the common sum S from the 59-card
nodes.description: Once the hidden number opposite 59 is identified as 2, the common sum is determined directly. The shared sum is S = 59 + 2 = 61. This S must apply to all three cards.

nodes.concept: Solve hidden numbers using S − visible
nodes.description: Given a common sum S on a two-sided card, the hidden number on a card equals S minus the visible number on that card. This is because visible + hidden = S for each card. So the unknowns can be computed by subtraction once S is known.

nodes.concept: Compute hidden prime opposite 44
nodes.description: Using S = 61, the hidden number opposite 44 is 61 − 44 = 17. This value is prime, consistent with the problem’s condition. So one hidden prime is 17.

nodes.concept: Compute hidden prime opposite 38
nodes.description: Using S = 61, the hidden number opposite 38 is 61 − 38 = 23. This value is prime, consistent with the problem’s condition. So another hidden prime is 23.

nodes.concept: Average of the hidden primes
nodes.description: The average (arithmetic mean) of three numbers is their sum divided by 3. After identifying the three hidden primes, you add them and divide by 3. This yields a single value summarizing the set.

nodes.concept: Compute the final average value

nodes.description: Many counting problems ask for the number of possible outcomes of a process. An outcome is one complete result of performing the entire procedure. Counting can often be done without listing outcomes explicitly by using systematic principles.

nodes.concept: Rule of product (multiplication principle)

nodes.concept: Radius and diameter relationship
nodes.description: In a circle, the diameter is the distance across the circle through its center, and the radius is the distance from the center to the circle. The diameter is always twice the radius. Equivalently, the radius is half the diameter.

nodes.concept: Area formula for a circle
nodes.description: The area of a circle is determined solely by its radius. The formula is A = πr^2, where r is the radius and π is the constant relating circumference to diameter. Squaring the radius means area grows quadratically with radius.

nodes.concept: Interpreting “k times the radius” scaling

nodes.concept: Shaded region as area difference

nodes.concept: Symmetric-sum substitution idea
nodes.description: When a system of equations is symmetric in x, y, z, it is often effective to replace the variables with elementary symmetric sums. The most common are s1 = x+y+z, s2 = xy+yz+zx, and s3 = xyz. Many symmetric polynomials in x, y, z can be rewritten in terms of these sums.

nodes.concept: Distributive expansion technique
nodes.description: Products of sums can be expanded systematically using distributivity: multiply each term in the first sum by each term in the second sum and then combine like terms. nodes.concept: Identity for (x+y+z)(xy+yz+zx)

nodes.concept: Root of a polynomial (definition)

nodes.concept: Vieta’s formulas (general idea for cubics)

nodes.concept: Function evaluation
nodes.description: Evaluating a function means substituting a given input into the function’s formula and simplifying. The output depends on algebraic substitution and respecting any domain restrictions (e.g., denominators cannot be zero). This is a core skill for working with explicit function definitions.

nodes.concept: Inverse function meaning
nodes.description: For an invertible function f, the inverse f^{-1} reverses f: f^{-1}(y) is the value x such that f(x)=y. Equivalently, f(f^{-1}(y))=y and f^{-1}(f(x))=x (when both sides are defined). This lets you translate statements involving f^{-1} into equations involving f.

nodes.concept: Translating equality involving inverse
nodes.description: If an equation has the form x = f^{-1}(y), then applying f to both sides yields f(x)=y (provided x is in the domain of f and y is in the range of f). nodes.concept: Rational expressions and domain exclusions
nodes.description: When an expression has a denominator, values that make the denominator zero must be excluded because the expression is undefined there. When solving equations, these excluded values can appear as “extraneous” candidates if you multiply both sides by expressions that could be zero. nodes.concept: What a recurrence defines
nodes.description: A recurrence relation defines each term of a sequence using earlier terms. To compute or compare terms, you repeatedly substitute the recurrence as needed. Understanding which earlier indices are referenced is key to controlling the computation.

nodes.concept: Shifting (re-indexing) a recurrence
nodes.description: If a recurrence holds for all n beyond some point, it also holds when you replace n by n-1, n-2, etc., as long as indices remain valid. Writing the recurrence for consecutive indices often reveals cancellations. This is a standard technique to derive simpler relations.

nodes.concept: Combining two recurrences to eliminate terms
nodes.description: Adding or subtracting two shifted versions of a recurrence can cancel shared intermediate terms. The goal is to reduce the number of different indices involved, ideally to a direct relation between far-apart terms. This creates a simpler recurrence that is easier to iterate.

nodes.concept: Deriving the relation x_n + x_{n-1} = x_{n-1} - x_{n-5}
nodes.description: Write the recurrence for x_n and for x_{n-1}, then add them term-by-term. The terms involving x_{n-2}, x_{n-3}, and x_{n-4} cancel in pairs, leaving x_n + x_{n-1} on the left and x_{n-1} - x_{n-5} on the right. This intermediate identity is the key bridge to a very short recurrence.

nodes.concept: Concluding x_n = -x_{n-5}

nodes.concept: From sign-flip to 10-step repetition

nodes.concept: Reducing indices using period 10
nodes.description: If x_n = x_{n-10}, then x_n depends only on n modulo 10. To find x_k for large k, repeatedly subtract 10 until you land in the range of known/computeable early terms. This converts the problem from huge indices to small-index evaluations.

nodes.concept: Mapping 531, 753, 975 to small indices

nodes.concept: Computing x_5 from the original recurrence

nodes.concept: Displacement vs. path length
nodes.description: A multi-step walk can be summarized by its net displacement: the single vector from start to end. The total path length adds every segment, but the distance from the starting point depends only on the final position relative to the start. Understanding the problem requires focusing on where Stacey ends up, not how far she walked in total.

nodes.concept: Cardinal directions as opposite signs
nodes.description: Opposite directions on the same line can be treated as having opposite signs (e.g., west vs. east, north vs. south). This lets you combine movements by adding signed values rather than tracking each step separately. Choosing a consistent convention (e.g., west and north positive) makes net movement easy to compute.

nodes.concept: Orthogonal axes for north/south and east/west
nodes.description: North–south movement and east–west movement occur along perpendicular (orthogonal) axes. Because they are independent components, you can compute the net change in each direction separately. The final displacement vector is fully determined by these two perpendicular components.

nodes.concept: Net component from multiple segments
nodes.description: To find the net displacement component along one axis, combine all segments along that axis using addition for the same direction and subtraction for opposite direction. This reduces multiple moves to a single equivalent move in that axis. You do this separately for the west/east axis and for the north/south axis.

nodes.concept: Combining same-direction horizontal steps in this problem
nodes.description: In the given walk, both horizontal moves are to the west: 11 meters west and 4 meters west. Since they are in the same direction, they add directly. This yields a single horizontal displacement of 15 meters west.

nodes.concept: Combining opposite-direction vertical steps in this problem
nodes.description: The vertical moves are 30 meters north and 22 meters south, which are opposite directions on the same axis. The net vertical displacement is found by subtracting the smaller from the larger: 30 − 22. This gives a net of 8 meters north.

nodes.concept: Right triangle formed by perpendicular displacement components
nodes.description: When you have a horizontal displacement and a vertical displacement that are perpendicular, they form the legs of a right triangle. The straight-line distance from start to end is the hypotenuse of that triangle. Thus, the problem reduces to computing the hypotenuse from the two net components.

nodes.concept: Pythagorean theorem for distance
nodes.description: For a right triangle with legs a and b, the hypotenuse c satisfies c = sqrt(a^2 + b^2). This theorem converts perpendicular component lengths into a single straight-line distance. It is the standard method for distance in a 2D grid with orthogonal axes.

nodes.concept: Set up distance expression with this problem's components
nodes.description: After simplifying the walk, the net displacement components are 15 meters west (horizontal) and 8 meters north (vertical). Since these are perpendicular, the distance from the starting point is sqrt(15^2 + 8^2). This expression directly applies the Pythagorean theorem to the computed components.

nodes.concept: Compute the numerical distance
nodes.description: Compute 15^2 = 225 and 8^2 = 64, then add to get 289. Taking the square root gives sqrt(289) = 17. Therefore the straight-line distance from the start is 17 meters.

nodes.concept: Final conclusion in context
nodes.description: Stacey ends 15 meters west and 8 meters north of where she started. The straight-line distance between these two points is 17 meters. Thus, she is 17 meters from her starting point.

nodes.concept: Right triangle definition
nodes.description: A right triangle is a triangle with one angle measuring 90 degrees. The side opposite the 90-degree angle is called the hypotenuse. The other two sides are the legs.

nodes.concept: Hypotenuse is the longest side
nodes.description: In any right triangle, the hypotenuse is longer than either leg. This follows from Euclidean geometry and is consistent with the Pythagorean relationship. Therefore, identifying the longest side helps identify the right angle’s opposite side.

nodes.concept: Longest side opposite largest angle
nodes.description: In any triangle, larger angles are opposite longer sides, and the longest side is opposite the largest angle. This provides a way to compare angles by comparing side lengths when some side lengths are known. It is commonly used to rule out which angle could be the right angle.

nodes.concept: Read triangle data and compare given side lengths
nodes.description: From the problem statement, side lengths are BC = 2 and AC = 4, so AC > BC. This comparison indicates AC is the longer of those two sides. Such comparisons are used to determine which side could be the hypotenuse.

nodes.concept: Determine which angle is the right angle using the hypotenuse
nodes.description: If an angle is 90 degrees, it must be opposite the hypotenuse (the longest side). Since AC is longer than BC, AC is more plausible as the hypotenuse than BC. Therefore, the right angle cannot be opposite BC, ruling out ∠A as the right angle in this labeling.

nodes.concept: Conclude ∠B is the right angle and AC is the hypotenuse
nodes.description: Because ∠A cannot be the right angle (it would force BC to be the hypotenuse, contradicting BC < AC), the right angle must be at B. That means AC is the hypotenuse. The remaining sides AB and BC are the legs.

nodes.concept: Pythagorean Theorem statement
nodes.description: For a right triangle with legs of lengths a and b and hypotenuse c, the Pythagorean Theorem says a^2 + b^2 = c^2. This theorem applies only when one angle is 90 degrees. It is used to compute an unknown side when the other two are known.

nodes.concept: Map triangle sides to Pythagorean roles
nodes.description: Once the right angle is identified, the side opposite it is the hypotenuse (c), and the other two sides are legs (a and b). Here, with ∠B right, AC is the hypotenuse and AB and BC are the legs. Correct mapping is necessary before substituting into a^2 + b^2 = c^2.

nodes.concept: Set up the specific Pythagorean equation
nodes.description: Using the mapping, AB^2 + BC^2 = AC^2. Substituting the known values gives AB^2 + 2^2 = 4^2. This creates an equation in the single unknown AB.

nodes.concept: Solve for AB^2 numerically
nodes.description: Compute the squares: 2^2 = 4 and 4^2 = 16. Then AB^2 = 16 − 4 = 12. This isolates the squared length of AB.

nodes.concept: Take square root to get AB length
nodes.description: Since AB is a side length, AB is positive. Taking the square root gives AB = √12. The next step is to express √12 in simplest radical form.

nodes.concept: Simplify radicals using perfect-square factors
nodes.description: To simplify √n, factor n into a product containing perfect squares, such as n = k^2·m. Then √n = k√m. This produces an equivalent expression with no perfect-square factor left under the radical.

nodes.concept: Apply radical simplification to √12
nodes.description: Factor 12 = 4·3, so √12 = √(4·3) = 2√3. This is simplest radical form because 3 has no square factor greater than 1. Therefore AB = 2√3.

nodes.concept: Cosine parametrization for x in [-1,1]
nodes.description: Any real number x with -1 ≤ x ≤ 1 can be represented as x = cos θ for some angle θ in [0°, 180°]. This substitution is useful because it converts expressions involving x and √(1−x²) into trigonometric functions of a single parameter.

nodes.concept: Relationship between sin and √(1−cos²θ)
nodes.description: If x = cos θ with θ in [0°, 180°], then √(1−x²) = √(1−cos²θ) = |sin θ|. On [0°, 180°], sin θ ≥ 0, so √(1−x²) = sin θ without an absolute value.

nodes.concept: Law of Cosines as a length formula
nodes.description: In any triangle with sides a and b enclosing angle C, the opposite side c satisfies c² = a² + b² − 2ab cos C. This allows converting an expression of the form √(a²+b²−2ab cos C) into a concrete side length.

nodes.concept: Triangle Inequality for minimizing a broken path
nodes.description: For any triangle, the sum of lengths of two sides is at least the length of the third side: YZ + XZ ≥ XY. Geometrically, this means traveling from Y to Z to X cannot be shorter than traveling directly from Y to X.

nodes.concept: Equality condition in the Triangle Inequality
nodes.description: Equality in YZ + XZ ≥ XY occurs exactly when points Y, Z, X are collinear and Z lies on the segment overline{YX} (so the “broken path” is actually a straight segment). This condition is crucial to verify that a proposed minimum is attainable.

nodes.concept: Pythagorean Theorem for right triangles
nodes.description: In a right triangle with legs p and q and hypotenuse r, we have r² = p² + q². This is used to compute a fixed distance when two perpendicular segments are known.

nodes.concept: Complementary angles: cos(90°−θ)=sin θ
nodes.description: For any angle θ, the cosine of its complement equals the sine: cos(90°−θ) = sin θ. This identity lets a Law of Cosines expression involving cos(90°−θ) be rewritten in terms of sin θ.

nodes.concept: Strategy: realize radicals as side lengths to minimize a path
nodes.description: A common minimization strategy is to interpret each radical √(…) as the length of a side in a triangle produced by the Law of Cosines. Then the sum of radicals becomes a sum of two side lengths (a broken path), which can often be bounded below by the Triangle Inequality.

nodes.concept: Constructing a geometric configuration with fixed sides and angle θ
nodes.description: Choose points O, X, Y such that OX and OY are perpendicular, and introduce a point Z so that OZ has fixed length 7, while angles with OZ match θ and 90°−θ. This setup is designed so that triangles YOZ and XOZ have angles that allow the Law of Cosines to produce the given radical forms.

nodes.concept: Angle assignment from x = cos θ and √(1−x²)=sin θ
nodes.description: After substituting x = cos θ, the expression √(1−x²) becomes sin θ, so the problem depends on θ. The construction picks ∠YOZ = θ so that cos θ appears in one Law of Cosines computation, and ∠XOZ = 90°−θ so that sin θ appears in the other.

nodes.concept: Computing YZ from triangle YOZ via Law of Cosines
nodes.description: In triangle YOZ with OY = 3, OZ = 7, and included angle ∠YOZ = θ, the Law of Cosines gives YZ = √(3² + 7² − 2·3·7 cos θ). Substituting cos θ = x turns this into YZ = √(58 − 42x), matching the first radical.

nodes.concept: Computing XZ from triangle XOZ via Law of Cosines
nodes.description: In triangle XOZ with OX = 10, OZ = 7, and included angle ∠XOZ = 90°−θ, the Law of Cosines gives XZ = √(7² + 10² − 2·7·10 cos(90°−θ)). Using cos(90°−θ)=sin θ and sin θ = √(1−x²) yields XZ = √(149 − 140√(1−x²)), matching the second radical.

nodes.concept: Rewriting the objective as YZ + XZ
nodes.description: Once the radicals are identified as lengths YZ and XZ in the constructed figure, the original expression becomes the path length from Y to Z to X. Thus the minimization problem becomes minimizing YZ + XZ over permissible placements of Z induced by θ.

nodes.concept: Lower bound: YZ + XZ ≥ XY
nodes.description: By the Triangle Inequality in triangle YXZ, the sum YZ + XZ is at least the direct distance XY. Therefore, no matter what θ (and hence Z) is, the expression cannot be smaller than XY.

nodes.concept: Computing XY from right triangle XOY
nodes.description: Because the construction makes ∠XOY = 90° with OX = 10 and OY = 3, triangle XOY is right. The Pythagorean Theorem gives XY = √(10² + 3²) = √109.

nodes.concept: Attainability: choosing Z on segment XY with OZ=7
nodes.description: The lower bound becomes the actual minimum if equality in the Triangle Inequality is achievable, i.e., if Z can lie on segment XY. The construction asserts that equality occurs when Z is on overline{XY} and simultaneously satisfies OZ = 7, which makes YZ + XZ = XY.

nodes.concept: Conclusion: minimum value equals √109
nodes.description: Since the expression equals YZ + XZ, it is bounded below by XY = √109, and that bound is achievable under the stated equality condition. Therefore the minimum possible value of the original expression is √109.
